[h1]Cooler Genremix, der unter gravierenden Schwachpunkten leidet[/h1]
Legie ist ein cooler Mischmasch aus Adventure und Dungeon Crawler im düsteren Mittelalter-Setting. Der Mix harmonisiert dabei überraschend gut und bietet dem Spieler knifflige aber logisch nachvollziehbare Inventarrätsel und finstere Minen-Dungeons mit Grusel-Flair.
Es ist eines dieser Spiele, denen ich wirklich gerne eine gute Wertung geben würde. Dummerweise gibt es gravierende Macken, welche mir dies unmöglich machen. Softlocks waren bereits in den 90ern ein No Go und die Kämpfe mit ihrem primitiven Stunlock-Geklicke machen keinen Spaß. Obendrein versucht das Spiel seine kurze Spieldauer mit jeder Menge Backtracking zu kaschieren. Am schlimmsten war jedoch mit Abstand das völlig unfaire Schlussrätsel, welches wohl niemand ohne Komplettlösung lösen wird. Selbst der Autor der Komplettlösung musste beim Entwickler nachfragen, um das Spiel endlich durchspielen zu können. An diesem Punkt war mein guter Wille dann wirklich erschöpft und es gab die Abwertung in den durchschnittlichen 6 von 10 Punkte-Bereich. Hätte nicht sein müssen. Für den sehr günstigen Preis können Interessierte dennoch zugreifen (daher auch der blaue Daumen).


[h1]Pro und Kontra:[/h1]

Pro:
- cooler Low-Poly-Grafikstil im Stil der Spät-90er
- düster-atmosphärisches Mittelalter-Setting

Kontra:

- beinhaltet Softlocks bzw. „Dead Man Walking“-Gefahren

LEGIE is an unusual, deeply personal indie title that stands apart from most Steam releases through its uncompromising focus on atmosphere, tone, and narrative oddity rather than conventional mechanical polish. Developed and published by the solo creator Spytihněv, the game drops players into a bleak medieval setting inspired by Central European folklore and sensibilities, immediately establishing a mood that feels grounded, miserable, and strangely intimate. Instead of heroic fantasy or epic stakes, LEGIE is concerned with small lives, bad decisions, and the quiet despair of people simply trying to get through another rainy day, and this thematic focus defines the entire experience.

The opening hours make it clear that LEGIE is not interested in traditional power fantasies. You begin as a lowly tavern worker burdened with menial tasks, abusive authority, and constant intoxication, all presented with a darkly comic edge that masks a deeper sense of hopelessness. Mundane chores like serving drinks or dealing with drunken patrons are not filler, but world-building tools that establish the social rot and emotional exhaustion that permeate the setting. When the story finally begins to spiral outward into quests, strange encounters, and supernatural hints, it feels less like the start of an adventure and more like a reluctant descent into problems you never wanted but cannot avoid.

Exploration in LEGIE is slow, deliberate, and often uncomfortable, using a tile-based movement system that emphasizes careful observation over fluid motion. Each step feels intentional, reinforcing the sense that the world is hostile and progress is never guaranteed. Locations are compact but densely packed with mood, from muddy outskirts littered with corpses to dim interiors where silence speaks louder than dialogue. The limited scale works in the game’s favor, as it encourages players to absorb details, revisit locations with new context, and treat the environment as an extension of the narrative rather than a backdrop for action.

Combat exists, but it is intentionally awkward and often unsatisfying in a traditional sense, reflecting the game’s broader themes of vulnerability and imbalance. Early encounters can feel brutally unfair, with limited tools and little room for tactical expression, creating moments of frustration that may deter players expecting a conventional dungeon crawler. As equipment improves, combat swings in the opposite direction, becoming almost trivial, which further highlights that fighting is not meant to be the core appeal. Instead, combat functions as another expression of LEGIE’s worldview: violence is either overwhelming or meaningless, rarely heroic, and never elegant.

Where LEGIE truly excels is in its storytelling and tonal consistency. The dialogue is laced with cynicism, gallows humor, and an undercurrent of resignation that gives even minor interactions weight. Characters feel tired, bitter, or broken, and the choices you make often reflect shades of apathy or reluctant compassion rather than clear moral victories. The narrative is not afraid to dwell on unpleasant subjects such as addiction, death, and societal decay, yet it never feels exploitative, instead presenting these elements as natural consequences of the world it portrays. This grounded, almost literary approach gives the game a lasting emotional impact that lingers well beyond its relatively short runtime.

Visually, LEGIE is modest and deliberately constrained, using a grid-based presentation and simple assets that recall older dungeon crawlers and experimental indie projects. While technically limited and occasionally restrictive due to its windowed presentation, the visuals serve the atmosphere effectively, allowing lighting, color, and composition to carry emotional weight. The minimalistic approach reinforces the sense of isolation and claustrophobia, making the world feel oppressive without needing graphical complexity. Sound design further enhances this mood, favoring subtle ambience and silence over constant musical reinforcement, which makes the environment feel uncaring and real.

In the end, LEGIE is not a game designed to please everyone, nor does it attempt to smooth over its rough edges. It is an introspective, melancholy experience that prioritizes mood, narrative voice, and thematic coherence over mechanical depth or accessibility. Players willing to approach it with patience and an openness to discomfort will find a deeply distinctive work that feels more like a personal statement than a product. LEGIE may be small, uneven, and occasionally frustrating, but its commitment to its vision makes it a memorable and thought-provoking journey that stands out in the indie landscape precisely because it refuses to conform.

La historia, ambientada en el pueblo medieval de [i] Jilemnice [/i] -Bohemia-, combina elementos oscuros y bizarros, que viran en torno a una taberna y a un trasfondo demoníaco. Si bien la trama es fácil de seguir, los diálogos pueden resultar curiosos o sin sentido, probablemente ligado a problemas de traducción.

This is a game that is kind of difficult to rate, it's a pretty bite sized adventure game that can be finished in an evening or two. You will navigate the world in a point and click interface to interact with objects and to solve puzzles, as well as talk to and interact with different NPCs. The art style is interesting and I found some charm in its pixelated blockiness. There's also combat inside the game's dungeons which although slightly clunky weren't frustrating in a way that ruined the enjoyment of the gameplay.

I'd imagine if you're the kind of person who hates looking at a guide Legie could give you some problems, some of the solutions are a bit obscure and the low poly environment sometimes can make it hard to find where you need to specifically interact with something to keep moving forward, but in general the logical flow of your activities make sense. You'll start your adventure in a medieval Czech town as a barkeep and slowly unravel more about the world around you, the world is quite dreary and macabre but there's plenty of dialogue that doesn't take itself too seriously and sort of leans into the surreal weirdness of the world that's created. The sound effects are minimal and yet there's still a cozy atmosphere and fun to be had in the adventure despite some of the point and click elements being a little bit clunky.

For $2 this is definitely an interesting thing to pick up if you want a different, surreal kind of adventure game that feels like it could have came out back in the PS1 days. There's not some amazing complex narrative here but the developments and interesting escalations in the story kept me wanting to see what would happen to our MC Jack. If you're on the fence get it on sale and don't be afraid to look up a guide since these point and click kind of games can be cryptic.

LEGIE is a weird one for me. For while it's a perfectly competent game in most aspects, I did leave with a shallow sense of disappointment overall.
That's not to say that I didn't enjoy my time with the game, since I for the most part did. That's why I beat it. But I would leave a 'mixed' review instead if I could.


Firstly, the game seems to have some sort of identity crisis. At times it wants to be a dungeon crawler, meanwhile at other moments it seeks to be a point-n-click game, however neither really appeal since the game has you awkwardly hopping between the two. Aspects of one segment simply doesn't flow nicely into the other one.
Really could've been done better. Far from terrible, but not great executing either. Only apt.

The combat is generally bothersome, as it is essentially boils down to spam-clicking on the enemy faster than they can hit you. Before you can obtain a shield, dying is inevitable as surviving the first few enemies is entirely based on RNG.
The combat significantly improves once you get the shield, but it's at that point just below decent.

The point-n-click aspects vary a lot. I enjoyed figuring out most of the puzzles, whereas the other few were truly infuriating. Said puzzles unabashedly craves a walkthrough guide, as they're so unintelligible and obscure. True pixel-sniffing.
A specific puzzles has you walking clock-wise around in a hallway, and if you fail to immediately recognize it as a puzzle, then you'll be completely soft-locked and forced to retreat to your last [i]manual[/i] save. Obtusely infuriating.


I did find the premise of the world rather engaging. It evokes a lot of melancholic mystery and a general sense of bittersweet awe. Definitely my favourite part of the game.
If the extent of the explorable world was expanded, then that would've really appealed to me. As it does feel rather unnecessarily cramped in terms of scale. Still fun to waddle around in.
The environments were visually very appealing, and I honestly just enjoyed the look of the game a lot.
Specific songs were also quite nicely atmospheric. Seamlessly soaking into the background of gameplay.

The story did feel unfocused, and as if it didn't know what to do with itself for the majority of the game.
I enjoyed the initial premise, yet it quickly deviated. And the practically identical pair of endings certainly didn't help, as they both come suddenly out of nowhere. They just don't feel like a proper ending, especially since they go by so fast, and leave so many parts of the game unresolved.


Overall, yeah. I'm aware that I'm describing this game rather harshly. But I do think that it can be a fairly enjoyable experience to beat over the weekend, and then be done with. It's very much that type of game.
It's unfortunately not much more than that.

¿Alguna vez soñaste con ser camarero en un pueblo checo arrasado por la peste? Probablemente no, pero [b]LEGIE[/b] se toma el atrevimiento de introducirte en ese mundo oscuro. Así es, somos un camarero cuyo único fin es complacer a nuestro jefe atendiendo su taverna. El problema comienza cuando nos quedamos sin cerveza… y con palabras propias del desarrollador, [b]LEGIE[/b] trata sobre camareros, cervezas y el diablo. ¿Cómo se une todo eso? tocará descubrirlo.

Siendo un poco más preciso, [b]LEGIE[/b] es una aventura point-and-click con algo de dungeon crawler, pero poco. Su núcleo es encontrar el objeto correcto y usarlo donde corresponde. A veces es intuitivo y otras veces prácticamente imposible y esto nos abre la puerta a su mayor defecto. La falta de explicación en algunos momentos torna el juego en algo frustrante. En lo personal, no pude terminarlo sin usar una guía y comprendo que hice lo correcto porque nunca me hubiese dado cuenta de algunas cosas que tenía que hacer para avanzar. En contraparte, los combates son verdaderamente fáciles y las mazmorras relativamente simples. Otro punto negativo es que es fácil llegar a un “softlock” si no se gestiona bien el dinero, de modo que es importante guardar la partida en distintos slots.

Visual y sonoramente está bien. Dan esa sensación de estar metidos en un mundo oscuro donde solo pasan cosas malas. Hay diversos detalles en el escenario como mierda tirada en las calles y eso suma completamente a la inmersión. Los diálogos son algo particulares. No se si se debe a una traducción mala o sencillamente buscaron que fuese algo bizarro. Sea como sea, aporta su grano a hacer del mundo algo más deplorable.

[b]LEGIE[/b] es un juego recomendado, pero con defectos importantes. Afortunadamente se suele encontrar con descuento lo que lo vuelve bastante accesible. Su jugabilidad no es para todo el mundo y se recomienda tener una guía en mano para los momentos difíciles.

[h1]This place is cold and forsaken by God...[/h1]
[i]LEGIE[/i] is an odd game. A combination of grid-based dungeon crawler and 3D adventure game, the game's strengths lie in a powerful atmosphere. You click around on the game's screen to move automatically to the next "tile" (even if the game does a good job in some areas making them not actually feel like rigid tiles). Despite the game's brevity and relative lack of assets (the game is about fourteen megabytes in size), it manages to make the medieval Czech town of Jilemnice feel oppressive. Everything is falling to bits, and people would rather drink their sorrows away than face the world. That's where you, the assistant at a local tavern, come in. 

The game is perhaps strongest in its first ten minutes, where you are listening to the depressed miners and their stories, wiping vomit up from the floor, picking up chairs they've toppled over, and putting up with the would-be poet in the corner, trying desperately to earn a living. All the while your boss berates you for what a terrible job you're doing. It is a stellar opening to a game all about the misery of life and the temptation of greed. You really get the sense that the world has fallen apart outside your tavern - so when you get to step outside, it is quite cool to see those expectations fulfilled. 

The game "opens up" a little into a dungeon crawler with some combat, but it's not stand-out or anything. Once you get a shield, combat basically can't be lost. One plays [i]LEGIE[/i], then, not for the combat or the action, but for the world and the weird characters within it. It is that tangible sense of place and belonging that makes the game so worth diving into and playing for oneself. If you enjoy that kind of thing in video games, this is an easy recommendation. But for those looking for a solid dungeon-crawler will be disappointed - those elements are there, sure, but they aren't challenging. The dungeon crawling is more in service of the game's weirdly effective mood and tone. You're the only one being proactive about anything - everyone else is struck by deep malaise. 

Before I finish this review, however, it is worth noting the game can only be played in a 512 * 512 window, and cannot be made full screen. This may be a deal breaker for some - but let me say that the game is still incredibly immersive, even with this limitation. But if you like adventure games (and don't mind backtracking and sometimes scratching your head about what to do next), and/or you are nostalgic for 90s 3D polygons, you will find yourself having a fun, immersive time in [i]LEGIE[/i].

Czech dungeon crawler and slave simulator with soul. This is a weird little game that came out in 2007ish. You start as the employee (slave) of an inn keeper and then things take a turn for the adventerous. The age of the game clearly shows, but there is still many good ideas that make for an interesting (and sometimes frustrating) playthrough and the charm is undeniable. 

It works on fairly classic point and click logic and you play using your mouse. You move like in a classic dungeon crawler. There are some combat, but this is janky and not really important to the game. You will have to figure out how to progress mostly by yourself. Sometimes you will get a hint or order from an NPC, other times you need to explore and figure out some stuff on your own. Some of the things you have to think out are pretty satisfying to understand. Because of that people that like investigation/mystery games with little handholding might like this game. Most of the things you have to find do not require pixel hunting, but there is at least one thing that is kind of hard to get unless you know about it or just try everything. 

Music and sound effects are good enough. I think this game is translated from Czech which makes some of the dialogue interesting, to put it mildly. It adds to the surrealness of the game. 

TL;DR: Short charming old dungeon crawler with some puzzles. I will recommend it because it is such a different game to what most games are today and I think people should try it out even if it might not be the type of game you usually play. The price is low already, but if you get it on sale you probably won't regret it even if you get really frustrated or confused.

LEGIE is definetly an interesting and unforgettable experience which I find very funny despite it's grim atmosphere. The medieval times were rough and dirty and the game takes full advantage of that. I love the atmosphere: everything and everyone is ugly and dying or will be dying soon because life sucks and our protagonist have to find the solution to all the problems: a barrel of beer. And it turns out that it is easier to find literal gold in this area, than beer. 

A unique mix of point-and-click and dungeon crawler (with a little bit of survival elements) is an interesting combination that gets boring after a while because dungeons are very look-alike. But what really can drive you nuts is puzzles. I can't be too mad on the game for it though, because they make some sense and for MOST of them there're hints you can understand without a guide (achievements help a lot too, especially with mechanics that game don't explain to you at all). And some of them lead to interesting scenes. There's also trolling: you can softlock yourself a few times just because you don't know you need that gold coin or because you can't read signs, which is an interesting design desicion to say the least.

I think going through all of the slog worth it because of the ending. Some things get into perspective after it which is cool and the ending itself is what you probably don't expect in a good way. Overall, a good project that I totally won't forget any time soon.
